meaning.evidence: Every instruction survives, numbers intact: "It's 15F to 20F (9C-11C) degrees hotter in the sun", "Plan your day so you're not walking between 10am and 4pm", "cotton's great in the desert!", the rangers' snack list.

sense.evidence: Terms carry the sense: "you mightn't twig how much fluid you're losing", "not running out of puff" for avoiding fatigue, "Have a spell somewhere near shade", "staying out of strife" for avoiding hazards, "keep the tank full".

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian advice voice: "quick smart", "chuck in their day packs", "finish up late arvo", "the temperature can go through the roof". The heading keeps US "Stay Hydrated and Energized".

register.evidence: Level 3: the leaflet is retold in plain Aussie speech without piling on; "a simple but bloody effective way" is a single dad-level swear, within the brief.

tone.evidence: Keeps the upbeat, practical park-service tone, exclamations and all: "tasty tucker that's ready for the track!", "so don't skip this simple but vital way to cool down!"

flow.evidence: Reads like it was written that way: "Get going before sunrise and finish up late arvo."

variety.evidence: Good spread ("twig", "chuck", "tucker", "puff", "spell", "strife", "through the roof"), with "walk"/"walking" repeated as the stock replacement for hike.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the hike-smart guidance: hydration, salty snacks, timing, staying wet: "One of the best ways to keep your body temperature in check ... is to stay sopping wet."

problems.why: US spelling left in the heading.

sense.evidence: The few swaps mostly fit ("a late arvo finish", "bushwalkers"), but "cotton is ripper in the desert!" stretches 'great' (useful) into a cheer.

authenticity.evidence: What little Aussie there is sits on unchanged US prose: "offers unique challenges due to the combination of ambient temperature, elevation", "Stay Hydrated and Energized", "stay cool and energized", "the timing of their hike".

flow.evidence: Reads as the original does, but the swaps clash: "Experienced desert bushwalkers know that the timing of their hike".

variety.evidence: Only three Aussie items, "bushwalking" repeated: "Bushwalking in the Grand Canyon", "not bushwalking between", "while bushwalking".

B.summary: Essentially the original with a few words swapped; accurate but almost no Aussie.

meaning.evidence: All points kept, numbers intact: "It's 15F to 20F (9C-11C) degrees hotter in the sun", "not walking between the hours of 10am and 4pm", the snack list, "cotton is ripper in the desert!".

sense.evidence: Fits throughout: "hard yakka" for demanding, "you won't get buggered" for fatigue, "peckish", "staying out of strife", "keep the engine running", "sit out the worst of the heat".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Australian ranger: "a different beast", "your sweat dries off that quick you mightn't even realise", "chuck in their daypacks", "finish up late in the arvo".

register.evidence: Level 3: an easy Aussie retelling; "buggered" is a dad-level word within the brief.

tone.evidence: Keeps the friendly, practical leaflet tone: "Tasty tucker, and ready for the track!" "And remember, staying soaking wet isn't just about feeling better."

flow.evidence: Smooth spoken advice; one clunky join: "you'll have a heaps better time out on the tracks, and it'll be worth the effort".

C.summary: The most natural and varied version: complete, idiomatic, and true to the leaflet's tone.

meaning.evidence: All instructions survive, but it adds claims: "Now this is the trick I reckon most people miss.", "cooler and fresher than you'd ever expect", "it might just save your bacon", "Don't be one of them."

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "hard yakka", "salty snacks are the go", "won't end up buggered", "steering clear of heat exhaustion", "Simple as".

authenticity.evidence: Natural Aussie voice ("salty snacks are the go", "Simple as, and it works a treat"), but the frame lines are stock: "Now, this one's a ripper, and it might just save your bacon." "Can't argue with that!"

register.evidence: Heavier than level 3: a yarn frame and asides on every section ("Here's the thing.", "But here's the catch.", "And here's a number to think about."). No swearing past dad.

tone.evidence: The leaflet's upbeat practicality stays, but the showman patter ("It's like walking into an oven, a bit at a time.") makes it more of a pitch than a safety page.

flow.evidence: Reads aloud well, though the repeated lead-ins stack: "Here's the thing.", "But here's the catch.", "Now this is the trick".

variety.evidence: Wide range of slang: "save your bacon", "no stroll down the beach", "the go", "hard yakka", "peckish", "buggered", "strife", "works a treat".

essence.evidence: Recognisably the original, but the added framing ("Now, this one's a ripper") turns the leaflet into a fireside talk.
